You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

Please describe one finding for each of the studies mentioned in the document text.

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

name: read
content:
1	Video Game Play and Real-World Violence We must stop the glorification of violence in our society.
     2	This includes the gruesome and grisly video games that are now commonplace. It is too easy today for
     3	troubled youth to surround themselves with a culture that celebrates violence. —Donald Trump, U.S.
     4	President (2019) The tendency to link violent crimes to the playing of violent video games is so
     5	prevalent that a term exists to describe it: “the Grand Theft Fallacy.” As one might guess from the
     6	word fallacy, this tendency is not only flawed, it gets matters entirely backward. Countries that
     7	consume more video games have lower levels of violent crime than those devoid of this media (Markey
     8	and Ferguson 2017). Months when people play violent video games the most tend to be safer than
     9	months they play them less (Markey, Markey, and French 2015). Even when violent video games, like
    10	Grand Theft Auto, were first released, there tends to be a decrease in violent crimes (Beerthuizen,
    11	Weijters, and van der Laan 2017). These findings have been replicated by psychologists, economists,
    12	and sociologists at various universities considering numerous other variables (cf. Cunningham,
    13	Engelstätter, and Ward 2016; Ward 2011). Most strikingly, these findings are not unique to violent
    14	video game play— other forms of violent media have also been linked to decreases in violent crime.
    15	Contrary to the fear that violent television poses a threat to our society, violent assaults, rapes,
    16	and murders all decrease when people are watching extremely violent television shows (Messner 1986).
    17	Even violent movies have been linked to declines in real-world violence. As with violent video
    18	games, years in which the most violent films were released saw decreases in violent crime, and crime
    19	consistently decreases in the days following the release of popular violent movies (Dahl and
    20	DellaVigna 2009; Markey, French, and Markey 2015). Regardless of the type of violent media—games,
    21	movies, or television shows—the research is consistent. When society is exposed to violent media,
    22	there is a reliable reduction in real-world violence. The reason why violent video game play (and
    23	other violent media) seems to reduce crime can be traced back to what criminologists call “routine
    24	activity theory” (Felson 1994). The simple notion behind this theory is this: For a violent crime to
    25	occur, a perpetrator must be in the same location as the victim, and this location tends to be free
    26	of those who would likely prevent the crime. Now, consider how playing many hours of video games may
    27	keep these potential criminals and victims entertained and off the streets. Male gamers in the
    28	United States spend a total of 468 million hours each month playing video games (Snider 2014). These
    29	hours constitute time during which at-risk individuals remain inside their homes, instead of being
    30	out on the streets. In this manner, video game play could serve as an effective crime-reduction
    31	strategy. No taxpayer money is needed. It naturally targets those individuals who are at the highest
    32	risk for committing violence or being victims of violence, and it appears to be working. Video Game
    33	Play and Aggression If you shoot somebody in one of these games, you don’t go to jail, you don’t get
    34	penalized in some way—you get extra points! This doesn’t mean that your child will go out into the
    35	world and shoot someone. But they do use more aggressive language, they do use more aggressive
    36	images, they have less ability to control their anger, and they externalize things in these violent
    37	ways. It’s absolutely not good. —“Dr. Phil” McGraw, television personality (2005) As illustrated by
    38	Dr. Phil’s quote, although some might not think video games cause violent homicides, they are still
    39	willing to believe that video game play, especially violent video game play, causes aggressive
    40	behaviors like punching others, fighting, or bullying. In this context, aggressive behaviors are
    41	actions committed by an individual intending to harm another individual. Although similar to violent
    42	behaviors like homicides, aggressive acts tend not to cause such extreme physical harm (Bushman et
    43	al. 2016). Much of the research purporting to support the claim that video games cause more minor
    44	forms of aggression has done little more than establish associations between self-reports of video
    45	game play and self-reports of feelings. Figure 2 provides some examples researchers have used to
    46	examine whether video games cause aggression. As we can see from these items, these studies do not
    47	examine real acts of aggression. Instead, these questionnaires attempt to measure aggression by
    48	using items that assess whether an individual might be “jerky” (that is, believing that to say
    49	something nasty about an individual behind his or her back is acceptable), antisocial, (as in, “I
    50	feel unsociable”), gossipy (as in “I have spread gossip about people I do not like”), or—oddly
    51	enough—conservative (like someone who might say, “Any nation should be ready with a strong military
    52	at all times”) (Krahé and Möller 2004; Anderson and Dill 2000; Greitemeyer 2019; Anderson et al.
    53	2004). Thus, the meaning and importance one can draw from such studies are extremely suspect. When
    54	video game researchers have conducted experiments, these studies have typically involved one group
    55	of participants who play a violent video game and another group who plays a nonviolent video game.
    56	After a short play session, participants’ aggressive thoughts or behaviors are assessed. Some
    57	researchers who have used this methodology found that individuals who play violent video games are
    58	more likely to expose others to loud irritating noises (Bushman and Gibson 2011), report feeling
    59	more hostile on a questionnaire (Anderson and Dill 2000), give longer prison sentences to
    60	hypothetical criminals (Deselms and Altman 2003), and even give hot sauce to people who do not like
    61	spicy food (Yang, Huesmann, and Bushman 2014). Importantly, many other researchers cannot replicate
    62	these effects (Kühn et al. 2019). So, even if these various experimental outcomes might be related
    63	to disagreeable thoughts, it is extremely questionable how well these responses translate to
    64	real-world aggressive behavior such as fighting, hitting, and bullying. Other scholars have raised
    65	both methodological and measurement concerns with studies examining aggression. For instance, one
    66	popular method, the competitive reaction time task (CRTT), measures how aggressive a person becomes
    67	after playing a violent video game by giving the player a chance to “blast” another person with an
    68	irritating noise. Specifically, participants are allowed to select both the duration and the
    69	intensity level (on a scale of zero to ten) of a white noise burst administered to another person.
    70	Unfortunately, no standardized scoring method exists for this measurement of aggression. Some
    71	researchers have scored aggression as the sum of the intensity and duration (Bushman and Gibson
    72	2011), the product of the intensity and duration (Bartholow, Sestir, and Davis 2005), the
    73	log-transformation of duration, ignoring the intensity (Anderson and Dill 2000), and even the square
    74	root of the duration score multiplied by the intensity score (Carnagey and Anderson 2005).
    75	Collectively, there are at least 147 different ways researchers have scored this measurement. Given
    76	all these permutations, one can make it appear as if video games increase aggression, decrease

76	all these permutations, one can make it appear as if video games increase aggression, decrease
    77	aggression, or have no effect on aggression even within the same sample (Elson et al. 2014). Looking
    78	past such methodical problems, numerous scholars have conducted meta-analyses to try to understand
    79	better how big an effect video games have on these mundane aggressive outcomes. On average, only 0.4
    80	percent to 4 percent of the variance in minor forms of aggression can be explained by violent video
    81	games (Ferguson 2015b; Hilgard, Engelhardt, and Rouder 2017). Keep in mind that this small effect is
    82	in reference to the effect of video game play on aggressive outcomes with minimal repercussions
    83	(e.g., giving hot sauce to another person who does not like spicy foods) that often have methodical
    84	issues (e.g., the CRTT) and are not direct measurements of real-world aggressive acts. Thus, the
    85	extremely small effect sizes linking violent video games to questionable proxy measurements of
    86	aggression found in many studies likely constitute an overestimate of any true effect video game
    87	play has on real-world aggressive behaviors.

- Bushman and Gibson 2011: Individuals who play violent video games "are more likely to expose others to loud irritating noises."
- Anderson and Dill 2000: Participants "report feeling more hostile on a questionnaire."

- Yang, Huesmann, and Bushman 2014: Participants "give hot sauce to people who do not like spicy food."
- Kühn et al. 2019: "Importantly, many other researchers cannot replicate these effects."
- Bartholow, Sestir, and Davis 2005: Scored aggression "as the product of the intensity and duration."
- Carnagey and Anderson 2005: Scored aggression as "the square root of the duration score multiplied by the intensity score."
- Elson et al. 2014: "One can make it appear as if video games increase aggression, decrease aggression, or have no effect on aggression even within the same sample."
